documents.title: Global Alliance to Improve Outcomes in Acne management of acne update

chunks.content: Introduction Acne vulgaris (AV) is one of the most prevalent skin conditions globally, affecting approximately 85% of adolescents and young adults, with persistence into middle age in up to 50% of cases (Tan and Bhate ; Zaenglein et al. ). This chronic inflammatory disorder of the pilosebaceous unit manifests as comedones, papules, pustules, and nodules, often leading to scarring. Beyond physical symptoms, AV significantly impacts psychological well-being, with studies reporting depression in 10–20% and anxiety in 15–25% of affected individuals, contributing to reduced quality of life and poor self-image (Hazarika and Archana ; Bagatin et al. ). The chronicity of AV stems from multiple pathophysiological factors, including follicular hyperkeratinization, excess sebum production, Cutibacterium acnes overgrowth, and inflammatory processes (O’Neill and Gallo ). Management of AV varies by severity. Mild cases often respond to topical treatments such as retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, or antibiotics (Zaenglein et al. ). Moderate to severe cases typically require oral antibiotics, which have been a cornerstone of therapy for over 50 years. Among these, tetracycline-class antibiotics like doxycycline and minocycline are widely used due to their dual antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties (Garner et al. ; Asai et al. ; Del Rosso et al. ). Doxycycline, a second-generation tetracycline, exerts bacteriostatic effects against C. acnes and anti-inflammatory actions by inhibiting matrix metalloproteinases, downregulating pro-inflammatory cytokines, and reducing neutrophil chemotaxis, as demonstrated in clinical studies (Skidmore et al. ; Bahrami et al. ; Kelhälä et al. ). Clinical guidelines recommend doxycycline doses of 50–200 mg daily for 8–12 weeks, though extended use is common in practice (Tan et al. ; Zaenglein et al. ; Thiboutot et al. ). Despite its widespread use, the evidence base for doxycycline in acne vulgaris (AV) treatment remains fragmented. Notably, comparative evaluations against newer agents such as azithromycin—with its favorable pulse-dosing—are limited, and long-term safety data are sparse (Parsad et al. ; Kus et al. ; Babaeinejad et al. ). Reported adverse events, particularly gastrointestinal discomfort and photosensitivity, further underscore the need for reappraisal (Ullah et al. ; Cao et al. ). With the global surge in antimicrobial resistance, dermatology guidelines increasingly call for optimized antibiotic stewardship (Barbieri et al. ). Furthermore, heterogeneity in dosing regimens, treatment duration, and the use of adjunctive topicals complicates therapeutic decision-making. While prior reviews have broadly covered oral antibiotics (Garner et al. ; Bienenfeld et al. ), a comprehensive synthesis focused specifically on doxycycline’s comparative efficacy and safety—especially in relation to alternatives like azithromycin, metformin, and isotretinoin—is lacking. (Sadati et al. , Agrawal et al. , Nagar C , Raees et al. ). This systematic review and meta-analysis addresses this gap by evaluating data from randomized controlled trials to inform clinical practice and identify priorities for future research, including optimal dosing and long-term risk profiles. Methods Study design This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The protocol followed a predefined methodology encompassing database search, study selection, data extraction, risk of bias assessment, and quantitative synthesis. Eligible studies were restricted to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the efficacy and/or safety of oral doxycycline for the treatment of acne vulgaris (AV). The primary outcomes of interest were: treatment success, as defined in each included study based on criteria for clinically meaningful improvement (e.g., ≥ 50% reduction in lesion count or improvement on the Investigator’s Global Assessment [IGA] or Patient Global Assessment [PGA] scales); change in inflammatory lesion count; and change in Global Acne Grading System (GAGS) scores. The secondary outcome was the incidence and type of reported adverse events. Search strategy A comprehensive literature search was conducted across six electronic databases: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar, covering records from the inception of each database through March 2024. Google Scholar was included to broaden the scope despite its limitations in reproducibility, with results manually screened for consistency. The search strategy combined Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and relevant free-text terms, including “doxycycline,” “acne vulgaris,” “tetracycline,” “oral antibiotics,” “treatment,” “therapy,” and “efficacy,” linked using Boolean operators (e.g., “doxycycline AND acne vulgaris”). Filters were applied to restrict results to randomized controlled trials where applicable. Reference lists of all included studies and relevant review articles were manually screened to identify additional eligible publications. Grey literature, including conference abstracts, was also considered, but only included if full RCT data were available. Eligibility criteria Studies were included if they were RCTs involving patients with acne vulgaris (AV) of any severity, used oral doxycycline as an intervention, included a comparator arm (e.g., placebo, other antibiotics, or alternative treatments), reported at least one predefined outcome (efficacy or safety), and were published in English. Eligibility criteria Studies were included if they were RCTs involving patients with acne vulgaris (AV) of any severity, used oral doxycycline as an intervention, included a comparator arm (e.g., placebo, other antibiotics, or alternative treatments), reported at least one predefined outcome (efficacy or safety), and were published in English. Exclusion criteria encompassed secondary studies (e.g., systematic reviews, meta-analyses), non-English publications, studies not involving doxycycline, studies including participants with conditions other than AV, studies without a comparator arm, or those not reporting predefined outcomes. The exclusion of non-English studies may introduce language bias, which is acknowledged as a limitation in the discussion. Data extraction Two independent reviewers extracted data using a standardized template (available as a supplementary file), capturing the first author’s name, publication year, sample size, sex distribution, intervention details (doxycycline dose, frequency, duration), comparator details, and outcomes. Primary efficacy outcomes included treatment success (defined per each study’s criteria for significant acne severity improvement), change in inflammatory lesion count, and GAGS score changes. Safety outcomes comprised adverse events associated with doxycycline. Discrepancies in data extraction were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer consulted if consensus could not be reached. Risk of bias assessment The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (ROB-2) tool was used to evaluate the risk of bias in the included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) across five domains: (1) bias arising from the randomization process, (2) bias due to deviations from intended interventions, (3) bias due to missing outcome data, (4) bias in measurement of the outcome, and (5) bias in selection of the reported result. Each domain was rated as “low risk,” “some concerns,” or “high risk,” and an overall risk of bias judgment was assigned to each study accordingly. Two reviewers independently conducted the assessments, and any discrepancies were resolved through structured discussion or, if necessary, consultation with a third reviewer to ensure objectivity. A detailed summary of the risk of bias evaluations for each study is provided in Supplementary Table , allowing transparency of the quality assessment process and its contribution to the interpretation of study findings. Outcomes Primary outcomes assessed were treatment effectiveness (significant improvement in acne severity per study criteria), inflammatory lesion count changes, and GAGS score changes. Secondary outcomes included the frequency and types of adverse events associated with doxycycline treatment. Statistical analysis Meta-analyses were performed using Review Manager (RevMan 5.4). For binary outcomes (e.g., treatment success), odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. For continuous outcomes (e.g., inflammatory lesion counts, GAGS scores), mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs were computed. A random-effects model was employed due to expected heterogeneity arising from clinical and methodological variations across studies, including differences in participant populations (e.g., age, baseline acne severity), interventions (e.g., dosage, duration, comparator type), and outcome measurement tools. This model accounts for both within- and between-study variance, yielding more conservative and generalizable estimates. Heterogeneity was quantified using the I2 statistic, with thresholds of 25%, 50%, and 75% indicating low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively. Clinical heterogeneity (e.g., differences in acne severity or treatment protocols) was considered alongside statistical heterogeneity to interpret results. A p-value ≤ 0.05 was deemed statistically significant. Subgroup analyses were planned based on comparator type, acne severity, and treatment duration, subject to sufficient data availability. Sensitivity analyses excluded high-risk-of-bias studies to test result robustness. Narrative synthesis was used when meta-analysis was infeasible due to insufficient data or excessive clinical heterogeneity. Safety outcome gaps were qualitatively evaluated based on reported adverse events. Results Literature search outcomes The literature search initially identified 873 articles from electronic databases: PubMed/MEDLINE ( n = 253), Google Scholar ( n = 420), and ScienceDirect ( n = 200). Prior to screening, 560 duplicate records were removed, and 21 records were excluded as ineligible by automation tools, resulting in 292 records screened. Following title and abstract screening, 173 records were excluded as irrelevant, leaving 119 reports sought for retrieval. Of these, 19 reports could not be retrieved, and the remaining 100 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. After evaluation, 23 studies were included in the review. The excluded studies comprised 18 secondary studies (e.g., systematic reviews, meta-analyses), 5 non-English publications, 20 studies not using doxycycline as an intervention, 14 involving patients with conditions other than acne vulgaris (AV), 9 lacking comparator arms, and 11 not reporting the required outcomes (treatment efficacy, inflammatory lesion count, GAGS score, or adverse events). A PRISMA flow diagram summarizing the search and selection process is presented in Fig. . Characteristics of selected studies that met the inclusion criteria The systematic review encompassed 23 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) conducted across diverse geographical regions, including Canada, the United States, Turkey, India, Iran, Bangladesh, Indonesia, Singapore, Chile, and Pakistan. These studies collectively involved a pooled sample size of 2,672 patients with acne vulgaris (AV) of varying severity, ranging from mild to severe. All studies utilized oral doxycycline as an intervention, with dosages typically ranging from 20 to 200 mg daily and treatment durations spanning 6 weeks to 6 months. Comparators to doxycycline were heterogeneous, including oral isotretinoin, azithromycin, placebo, erythromycin, aminolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy, silymarin (alone or combined with doxycycline), montelukast, metformin, and lesion extraction, often in combination with topical treatments such as adapalene, benzoyl peroxide, tretinoin, or clindamycin. The male-to-female ratio varied across studies, with some reporting balanced distributions (e.g., Tan et al. : 115:18 for the doxycycline arm) and others showing a female predominance (e.g., Arooba et al. : 40:112 for the doxycycline arm); a few studies did not report sex distribution (e.g., Mudassir et al. ). Efficacy was assessed using diverse methods, including percentage change in lesion counts (inflammatory and non-inflammatory), Global Acne Grading System (GAGS) scores, Acne Severity Index (ASI), Michaelsson severity index, resolution or disappearance of lesions, and patient/clinician global assessments. Some studies also measured additional outcomes such as inflammatory markers or itch questionnaire scores. Detailed characteristics of the included studies—such as author, setting, intervention protocols, sample sizes, sex ratios, and efficacy evaluation methods—are summarized in Table . Risk of bias assessment outcomes All 23 included studies were randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and their risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (ROB-2) tool, which assesses five domains: D1 (bias arising from the randomization process), D2 (bias due to deviations from intended interventions), D3 (bias due to missing outcome data), D4 (bias in measurement of the outcome), and D5 (bias in selection of the reported result). Most studies exhibited a high overall risk of bias, primarily driven by a lack of blinding. Specifically, 16 studies (e.g., Parsad et al. ; Babaeinejad et al. ; Ullah et al. ) were rated as high risk in D4 due to the absence of blinding, which posed a significant concern for subjective outcomes such as patient-reported treatment efficacy or global acne severity assessments. Additionally, 5 studies (e.g., Parsad et al. ; Cao et al. ; Muzaffar et al. ) showed some concerns in D1 due to unclear randomization processes, and 1 study (Zaman et al. ) was rated high risk in D1 for potential randomization issues. Most studies (19 out of 23) were low risk in D2, indicating minimal deviations from intended interventions, and in D5, suggesting low risk of selective reporting. However, 3 studies (e.g., Cao et al. ; Haider et al. ; Sitohang et al. ) had some concerns in D3 due to incomplete outcome data. The risk of bias summary, detailing each study’s assessment across all domains, is presented in Fig. . Meta-analysis outcomes Effectiveness of doxycycline Five of the included studies (Iqbal et al. ; Mudassir et al. ; Muzaffar et al. ; Parsad et al. ; Ullah et al. ) reported data on the effectiveness of doxycycline compared to azithromycin in treating AV (Fig. ). The pooled analysis, based on a total of 326 patients (165 in the doxycycline group with 124 events and 161 in the azithromycin group with 117 events), demonstrated that doxycycline’s efficacy was comparable to azithromycin, with no statistically significant difference in the proportion of patients achieving effective treatment (odds ratio [OR] 1.28; 95% confidence interval [CI] [0.54, 3.04], p = 0.57). The analysis revealed moderate heterogeneity among the studies (I 2 = 60%, p = 0.04), as indicated by a tau 2 of 0.57 and a chi 2 test (χ 2 = 9.94, degrees of freedom [df] = 4, p = 0.04). The forest plot, presented in Fig. , visually illustrates these findings, with individual study odds ratios ranging from 0.31 (Muzaffar et al. ) to 4.56 (Ullah et al. ), reflecting variability in treatment responses, though the overall effect size remained non-significant (z = 0.56, p = 0.57). Changes in inflammatory lesion counts Three studies ( Kus et al. ; Sadati et al. ; Skidmore et al. ) reported data on changes in inflammatory lesion counts following treatment, involving a total of 125 patients (65 in the doxycycline group and 60 in the control group) (Fig. ). The pooled analysis showed no significant difference in the mean change in inflammatory lesion counts between doxycycline and controls (mean difference [MD] −0.71; 95% confidence interval[CI] [−8.61, 7.19], p = 0.86). Individual study results varied, with Kus et al. ( ) reporting a mean reduction of 19.25 (SD 3.138) for doxycycline versus 20.9 (SD 3.75) for controls; Sadati et al. ( ) showing 16.1 (SD 16.86) versus 10.35 (SD 9.49); and Skidmore et al. ( ) indicating 15.71 (SD 1.1) versus 8.16 (SD 1.23). The analysis exhibited substantial heterogeneity (I 2 = 97%, tau 2 = 43.43, χ 2 = 77.45, df = 2, p < 0.00001) , suggesting variability in study designs, populations, or outcome measurements. The forest plot, presented in Fig. , illustrates these findings, with the overall effect (z = 0.18, p = 0.86) indicating no significant difference between treatments. Changes in Acne Severity (GAGS Scores) Four studies (Ahsan et al. ; Morteza et al. [doxycycline vs. silymarin]; Nagar et al. ; Nicklas et al. ) assessed changes in acne severity using the Global Acne Grading System (GAGS), involving 259 patients (130 in the doxycycline group and 129 in the control group). The pooled analysis revealed that GAGS score improvements were significantly greater in the control groups compared to those treated with doxycycline (mean difference [MD] 1.76; 95% confidence interval [CI] [1.53, 2.00], p < 0.00001). Individual study results showed consistent trends: Ahsan et al. ( ) reported a mean GAGS reduction of 11.67 (SD 2.09) for doxycycline versus 14.04 (SD 1.78) for controls (azithromycin); Morteza et al. ( ) reported 12.5 (SD 1.5) versus 14.9 (SD 1.7) (silymarin); Nagar et al. ( ) reported 12.15 (SD 1.92) versus 14.55 (SD 1.54) (azithromycin); and Nicklas et al. ( ) reported 11.8 (SD 1.3) versus 13.1 (SD 1.5) (aminolaevulinic acid photodynamic therapy). The analysis showed moderate heterogeneity (I 2 = 53%, tau 2 = 0.03, χ 2 = 6.37, df = 3, p = 0.09), suggesting some variability in study designs or populations. The forest plot, presented in Fig. , illustrates these findings, with the overall effect (z = 14.75, p < 0.00001) confirming the significant difference favoring controls (Fig. ). Safety The incidence of adverse events (AEs) following doxycycline therapy was reported in a subset of the included studies, with variability in types and rates. Skidmore et al. ( ) observed that 46% of patients on doxycycline experienced treatment-related AEs compared to 32% on placebo, with common events including influenza, headache, and rash, leading to discontinuation in 7.6% of doxycycline-treated patients. Prasad et al. ( ) noted a 4.8% discontinuation rate due to photosensitivity. Nicklas et al. ( ) reported AEs in the doxycycline group, including scaling (43%), photosensitivity (17%), erythema (17%), and stinging/burning (17%), though the total incidence was not specified. Haider et al. ( ) found gastrointestinal AEs in 12% of doxycycline patients versus 4% with azithromycin, and dermatologic AEs in 4% of doxycycline patients (comparator not reported). Nagar et al. ( ) reported gastrointestinal AEs in 46% of doxycycline patients versus 20% with azithromycin. These study-specific AE rates highlight potential tolerability issues, though their clinical impact (e.g., on adherence) requires further investigation due to inconsistent reporting across trials. Discussion This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy and safety of doxycycline compared to other treatments for acne vulgaris (AV), encompassing 23 randomized controlled trials with 2,672 patients. These findings prompt a nuanced reconsideration of doxycycline’s role in multidisciplinary acne management. The meta-analysis revealed that doxycycline’s treatment effectiveness was comparable to azithromycin, with no significant difference (odds ratio [OR] 1.28; 95% confidence interval [CI] [0.54, 3.04], p = 0.57), aligning with prior studies by Kus et al. ( ) and Babaeinejad et al. ( ) that noted similar efficacy in moderate acne (Kus et al. ; Babaeinejad et al. ). This equivalence is critical amid growing concerns about antimicrobial stewardship and the overlap with infectious disease management (Barbieri et al. ). Azithromycin’s pulse-dosing regimen may improve adherence and reduce selection pressure for resistant organisms, a factor gaining importance (Del Rosso et al. ). Additionally, the analysis of inflammatory lesion count reduction showed no significant difference between doxycycline and controls (mean difference [MD] −0.71; 95% CI [−8.61, 7.19], p = 0.86), though this result warrants caution due to high heterogeneity (I2 = 97%) and limited reporting. Variability may stem from differences in baseline acne severity, inconsistent comparators, treatment durations (6 weeks to 6 months), and diverse evaluation methods across studies. Garner et al. ( ) reported a 40–60% reduction in inflammatory lesions with tetracycline-class antibiotics (Garner et al. ), yet the current findings do not support doxycycline outperforming other treatments. A notable finding was the superior improvement in Global Acne Grading System (GAGS) scores with control interventions compared to doxycycline (MD 1.76; 95% CI [1.53, 2.00], p < 0.00001), with moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 53%). Controls, including isotretinoin, silymarin combinations, and photodynamic therapy, may address multiple pathophysiological aspects of acne beyond doxycycline’s antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory effects (Shie Morteza et al. ; Sadati et al. ). This aligns with consensus guidelines advocating isotretinoin for severe acne (Zaenglein et al. ; Thiboutot et al. ). In terms of tolerability, safety data revealed distinct adverse event (AE) patterns with doxycycline. Compared to azithromycin, gastrointestinal (GI) disturbances were more frequent (46% vs. 20% in Nagar et al. ), consistent with known tetracycline-class side effects (Skidmore et al. ). Other AEs included photosensitivity (4.8–17%), scaling (43%), erythema (17%), and stinging/burning (17%) (Nicklas et al. ), which may affect patient adherence. Although previous reviews suggest doxycycline may be safer than minocycline with regard to rare severe AEs (e.g., lupus, hyperpigmentation (Bienenfeld et al. ), the GI and dermatologic side effects remain notable concerns. Treatment variability was another concern, with reported durations ranging from 6 weeks to 6 months and doses varying from 20 mg twice daily to 200 mg once daily, reflecting a lack of standardized treatment protocols. Despite guideline-based support for topical combinations (Zaenglein et al. ), their usage was inconsistent across studies. The commonly recommended regimen of 100 mg daily for 2–3 months (Asai et al. ), was observed in some trials, yet the optimal dose and duration remain unclear. This review also has several limitations. Many included studies exhibited high risk of bias, particularly due to inadequate blinding, which may have influenced subjective outcomes such as patient satisfaction. Inconsistencies in comparators, outcome measures, and study methodologies further limited comparability. Moreover, most studies assessed short-term outcomes (≤ 3 months), restricting conclusions on long-term efficacy and safety. Documentation of compliance, detailed adverse events, and patient-reported outcomes such as quality of life was limited. Clinically, azithromycin may be preferable for patients with GI sensitivities or frequent sun exposure due to doxycycline’s harsher side effect profile. For severe acne, isotretinoin remains a more effective option than prolonged antibiotic use. Clinicians should carefully counsel patients receiving doxycycline about photosensitivity and GI risks to improve adherence. Future randomized controlled trials should aim to optimize dosing strategies, evaluate newer or adjunct therapies, and include longer follow-up and patient-centered outcomes to address existing evidence gaps. Conclusion This systematic review and meta-analysis indicate that doxycycline’s effectiveness in treating acne vulgaris (AV) is comparable to azithromycin, with no significant difference (OR 1.28; 95% CI [0.54, 3.04], p = 0.57), and no notable difference in inflammatory lesion counts versus controls (MD −0.71; 95% CI [−8.61, 7.19], p = 0.86). However, control interventions significantly outperformed doxycycline in GAGS score improvements (MD 1.76; 95% CI [1.53, 2.00], p < 0.00001). Doxycycline was associated with higher adverse event rates, including GI issues (46% vs. 20% vs. azithromycin), photosensitivity (4.8–17%), scaling (43%), erythema (17%), and stinging/burning (17%), suggesting a less favorable safety profile. High heterogeneity (I 2 up to 97%) and bias from inadequate blinding, especially for subjective outcomes, temper result reliability. Clinically, doxycycline remains viable but requires careful risk–benefit assessment, particularly for patients with GI or photosensitivity risks, favoring azithromycin or isotretinoin for severe cases. Future blinded RCTs are needed to refine dosing, compare newer treatments, and assess long-term outcomes. Supplementary Information Below is the link to the electronic supplementary material.
